idiom_name: AnyVal value class / opaque type (wrapper erased at compile time)
implementation_notes: Scala's value classes exist 'to avoid allocating runtime objects': a class extending AnyVal with a single val parameter has that parameter as its runtime representation, and Scala 3's recommended replacement for the same job is the opaque type, which is likewise compile-time only. The documentation is explicit that allocation comes back when the value class is 'treated as another type' - used as a type argument (even identity), stored in an Array, or examined by a runtime type test - the same escape hatches Kotlin's inline classes have, so the optimization only holds along monomorphic, non-generic paths. This substitutes for a hand-rolled inline buffer in the wrapper case only; the JVM still cannot embed a variable-size payload in an object, so small byte payloads stay in Array[Byte]/ByteBuffer or off-heap memory, and @specialized/primitive arrays only remove boxing, not per-object allocation.
code_sketch:
final class Meters(val value: Double) extends AnyVal   // no Meters instance at runtime
def travel(d: Meters): Meters = new Meters(d.value + 1.0)

object Ids:                       // Scala 3: opaque type is the recommended form
  opaque type UserId = Long
  def apply(l: Long): UserId = l
  extension (u: UserId) def raw: Long = u

val xs = Array[Meters](new Meters(3.0))   // array assignment boxes: allocation returns
pitfalls: The documented allocation escapes are easy to hit: passing a value class as a type argument (List[Meters], identity), storing it in an Array, or pattern matching on it instantiates the wrapper, so 'no allocation' holds only until the value meets a generic or reflective boundary.

Value classes cannot have vals, vars, lazy vals, nested classes, secondary constructors or @specialized parameters, cannot be extended, and cannot wrap another user-defined value class; opaque types in Scala 3 lift most restrictions but expose no members, pushing the API into extension methods in the companion scope.

Universal traits and structural typing re-introduce allocation (any use as another type boxes), and equals/hashCode cannot be user-defined on a value class - so identity-sensitive logic must stay outside the wrapper.
sources: Scala documentation, Value Classes and Universal Traits - 'value classes are a mechanism in Scala to avoid allocating runtime objects', with the allocation cases (treated as another type, assigned to an array, runtime type tests) and the limitation list; Scala 3 recommends opaque types instead: https://docs.scala-lang.org/overviews/core/value-classes.html
Scala 3 documentation, Opaque Types - the recommended compile-time-only wrapper for the same purpose: https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/book/types-opaque-types.html
